about: Merge the crash-fix lanes into one map of SF crash groups to fixes, with people hurt and KSI avoided, cost per injury avoided and stacked packages.

effect.applies_to: Low: New York injury or fatal crashes IRR 0.96 (0.88 to 1.06). Mid: London KSI -12% by synthetic control. High: London all accidents -38% to -40% in the zone and charged hours (Green et al. 2014). Several London studies found more cyclist and motorcyclist casualties Dis-benefit to carry when stacking: several London studies found cyclist and motorcyclist casualties per km rose in some years as faster, emptier streets and more two-wheelers followed the charge.
effect.source: Green et al. 2014; Itzkowitz et al.; Li and Gao 2019, via crosscut lane and the downtown pricing note
effect.unit: % change in crashes or casualties in the charged zone (rows differ in severity)

effect.applies_to: Low: SF's own 20 mph blocks show no drop (821 blocks, 1.27 before correction, still 10% to 20% above expected after it) and SFMTA measured 0 mph median change on 9 corridors. Mid: Edinburgh, streets changed vs streets kept at 30 mph, casualties -10% (-19% to 0%); citywide vs control zones -20%, collisions -22%. High: Wales, casualties on 20 and 30 mph roads 2,344 in 2022 to 1,759 in 2024, -25.0%, before and after only (Senedd's England comparison puts the gap near 19 points)
effect.source: Kokka et al. 2024 (Edinburgh); Welsh Government, Police recorded road collisions 2024; SF methods-by-intervention note
effect.unit: % change in injuries (casualties or collisions) on the streets whose limit fell

effect.applies_to: Low: SF's 33 locations, injury crashes within two blocks on the camera street -9% (-23% to +8%) after the matched-street check. Mid: NYC locations with 2022 cameras, injuries and fatalities 14% fewer than control corridors, 2021 vs 2023, no range published. High: SF crashes involving someone walking -27% (-50% to -5%) by Empirical Bayes, -20% (-47% to +20%) after the check. France's national network: deaths and injury crashes -19.7% nationwide (Blais and Carnis 2015, via camera note)
effect.source: NYC DOT ASE Program 2024 Report p. 1 and pp. 19-20; SF outcomes section
effect.unit: % change in injury crashes (or injuries and deaths) near cameras against comparison streets

effect.applies_to: All crashes of equipped vehicles at 100% adoption, no adaptation. ETSC states mass ISA adoption would cut collisions about 30% and deaths about 20%; the Carsten-based range is per severity. Scale by the equipped share of SF vehicle-miles, which for an EU-style new-vehicle rule is near 0 in year one and grows with fleet turnover (about 15 to 20 years) [inference — mine]
effect.source: ETSC (speed lane); Carsten et al. estimates via search (speed lane); Lai, Carsten and Tate 2012 via rules note (crosscut lane)
effect.tag: [primary — read 2026-11-25] (ETSC, per speed lane); [web search — verify] (Carsten)
effect.unit: % change in crashes at full fleet adoption (mid: all collisions; low: advisory fixed ISA, fatal and serious; high: mandatory dynamic ISA, fatal)

fixes.how_it_works: The default limit on every street without a posted limit drops to 20 mph by law, so the whole residential network changes at once without a sign on every block.
fixes.name: Citywide default speed limit of 20 mph (Wales 2023, Edinburgh, Paris 30 km/h 2021, Toronto, Seattle, Bristol, Helsinki)
fixes.sf_evidence: On 821 dated 20 mph blocks, injury crashes ran 10% to 20% above expected after correcting for the method's lean; no drop (methods-by-intervention note, [DataSF ubvf-ztfx, 3t7b-gebn — queried 2026-11-24]). SFMTA measured 0 mph median change, +1 mph 85th percentile, on 9 corridors.
fixes.sf_now: State law (AB 43, 2021) lets SF cut 5 mph only street by street: 79 business-district corridors (48.5 miles) and 33 safety corridors (59.2 miles), and the Tenderloin's 20 mph zone (2021). A citywide 20 mph default needs a state bill.

fixes.how_it_works: Planters, posts, diverters or one-way pairs close each cell of side streets to through driving, so every home stays reachable but no route crosses the cell, and through traffic stays on the main streets that ring it.
fixes.name: Low traffic neighbourhood program: filter every residential cell ringed by main streets
fixes.notes: Furlong found no convincing difference by filter type for serious injuries, so physical filters SF can build did about as well as camera filters (circulation note).
fixes.sf_evidence: None for a cell. Slow Streets (corridor filters) on 19 streets: injury crashes 0.73 (0.58 to 0.88), 0.88 (0.64 to 1.12) without those with other changes, with traffic at 0.38 of before, so the fall looks like less traffic (2026-11-24-methods-by-intervention.mdx).
fixes.sf_now: None built as a cell. Duboce Triangle has an SFCTA-funded study ($250,000, 2025) that stalled on turn-ban objections; Page Street and the Slow Streets are corridor filters. Four trial cells (Duboce, two Bayview, Outer Sunset) are sketched in the repo's LTN designer.

ranking.evidence_grade: low: a simple before and after from an advocacy group's summary of police counts.
ranking.name: Stop-as-yield for people biking (Idaho or Delaware stop)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: two independent sources (Sweden, NYC) agree on about 30%, but a longer cycle raises pedestrian wait and red-light crossing.
ranking.name: Exclusive pedestrian phase (all-walk or scramble)

ranking.evidence_grade: low: the one citywide evaluation found about no injury effect.
ranking.name: Citywide signal retiming to the lower limit (NYC's 25 mph retiming, Franklin Street)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: US empirical Bayes CMFs rated 3 to 4 stars and a Danish handbook value, but the Danish authors say the gain is limited to junctions with poorly set clearance
ranking.name: Longer all-red clearance interval

ranking.evidence_grade: low to moderate: one strong controlled study (Edinburgh, design level 4) with a modest effect, several nulls (Belfast, Bristol, DfT schemes, Toronto's comparison), Wales before-and-after, and SF's own null.
ranking.name: Citywide default speed limit of 20 mph (Wales 2023, Edinburgh, Paris 30 km/h 2021, Toronto, Seattle, Bristol, Helsinki)

ranking.evidence_grade: high: several empirical Bayes studies at 4 to 5 stars agree on 9% to 19% fewer pedestrian crashes; does not help a pedestrian crossing against the signal.
ranking.name: Leading pedestrian interval (early walk signal)

ranking.evidence_grade: low: US CRFs from manuals and NYC naive before and after; diversion to nearby corners is unmeasured
ranking.name: Left-turn bans and directional median openings

ranking.evidence_grade: low: SF's own data and the BLA 2016 study find no effect without enforcement or design.
ranking.name: Lower posted limits (20 mph) without physical change

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: Danish handbook urban values; study count not printed
ranking.name: Curbed median on an urban street

ranking.evidence_grade: low for SF: strong effects but almost all from rural roads and motorways.
ranking.name: Corridor-wide camera enforcement: average-speed (point to point) or cameras in series along a whole street

ranking.evidence_grade: low: Edinburgh and Japan are controlled and find modest falls; SF's one zone shows none.
ranking.name: Neighbourhood-wide signed 20 mph zones (Tenderloin 2021, Japan Zone 30, Edinburgh, London boroughs)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: Danish and Swedish handbook values rest on two large US studies and Nordic studies; the Danish authors say results vary widely because most studies are small, and the effect at signals is smaller
ranking.name: Left-turn lane with a curbed channelising island

ranking.evidence_grade: low: NYC's controlled study shows an effect for hardened corners only; SF's paint shows none; Hoboken is uncontrolled and bundled.
ranking.name: Citywide daylighting: every corner, with posts where drivers ignore paint (Hoboken; NYC's 200 to 500 a year)

ranking.evidence_grade: low: the only crash effect is a 1980s before and after on RTOR adoption, read only via a search summary.
ranking.name: No turn on red (citywide or at signals with heavy walking)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: strong US empirical Bayes CMFs, but SF's own test found no change, so transfer to SF's grid is in doubt
ranking.name: Lane reduction (road diet), four lanes to two plus turn lane or bike lanes

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: a good EB study gives about 9%; the SF pilot's 25% is weak design.
ranking.name: Pedestrian countdown signals

ranking.evidence_grade: low: a city before and after with no control, normalized by modelled cyclist counts; total crashes at all treated junctions rose 25% as riding grew.
ranking.name: Fully split phase: a bike signal with its own green, separate from turning drivers

ranking.evidence_grade: low: the Danish figure pools before-after studies of mixed rigour, and SF's paint-and-post corridors show no change yet.
ranking.name: Corridor-wide calming of urban through streets (Danish trafiksanering: islands, narrowings, raised crossings and a lower limit along a whole street)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: Danish evaluations agree on a small effect, and a larger Danish study found no significant change.
ranking.name: Set-back car stop line (5 m) and bike box at signals

ranking.evidence_grade: low: wide range across foreign studies; fixed-time grids with many pedestrians may gain less
ranking.name: Traffic-responsive signals with dilemma-zone green extension

ranking.evidence_grade: low: the Danish handbook halves a pooled estimate from methodologically weak studies; no dooring-specific crash result.
ranking.name: Remove parking at corners and along door-zone bike lanes (daylighting, no-parking on the bike side)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: one large controlled before-and-after study (113 London LTNs, 2012-2024, rest of London as control), with injuries returning when LTNs were removed; but nothing tests SF's hills, and SF-size cells did about half as well (-22%).
ranking.name: Low traffic neighbourhood program: filter every residential cell ringed by main streets

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: Danish and Swedish handbooks agree on about 40%; studies older and European.
ranking.name: Raised crosswalk or raised intersection

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: a 4-star 1986 urban study and a Danish handbook value agree in direction; old data and the MUTCD warrant limit where it applies
ranking.name: Convert two-way stop or yield control to all-way stop

ranking.evidence_grade: high for area-wide calming elsewhere (Cochrane, London time series over 119,029 segments) but SF's own hump blocks show a small, uncertain effect.
ranking.name: Area-wide traffic calming: engineered 20 mph zones with humps, raised junctions and chicanes every block (London 1986-2006, Japan Zone 30 Plus, Dutch 30 zones)

ranking.evidence_grade: high: Danish large-sample before and after and a Belgian replication agree on about -80% for the target crashes; US CMFs agree in direction. Flashing-yellow-arrow permissive phasing is weaker and replacing protected-only with it raised left-turn crashes 3.4 times in Utah (CMF 9401)
ranking.name: Protected-only left-turn phase

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: Danish before-after and with/without studies agree; not tested in a US city.
ranking.name: Continuous sidewalk across side streets (raised entry, Danish 'overkørsel')

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: NYC's large program reports injury drops against comparison sites (method not published on the page) and DC/SF measured conflict and speed drops; no peer-reviewed crash study read.
ranking.name: Left-turn calming: hardened centerline, median extension, slow-turn wedge

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: many before-and-after and some controlled studies show site effects; network-level evidence (France, NYC, Montgomery County) is quasi-experimental, and SF's own result is not yet clear.
ranking.name: Citywide speed camera network dense enough that drivers expect one anywhere (NYC 2,200+ cameras in 750 school zones, France, Montgomery County corridors)

ranking.evidence_grade: high: three independent sources (Denmark, Sweden, US meta-analysis) agree on 18% to 32%.
ranking.name: Pedestrian refuge island or raised median

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: a good SF study for school crossings, but Sweden finds marking alone can raise pedestrian risk.
ranking.name: High-visibility (continental) crosswalk markings with advance yield lines

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: meta-analyses of controlled studies agree on 20% to 30% fewer injury crashes; SF's own result is consistent but within chance.
ranking.name: Speed humps, cushions and raised tables on residential streets (engineered 20 mph streets)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: a large Danish before and after study, reversed when tracks were extended again; riders report feeling less safe, and transfer to US turning volumes is untested.
ranking.name: Truncated cycle track before signalized junctions (Danish afkortet cykelsti)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: many controlled studies agree on fewer injury crashes near cameras; SF's own result points the same way but is within chance and KSI did not fall.
ranking.name: Fixed speed safety cameras (SF's 33 locations under AB 645)

ranking.evidence_grade: high: a 5-star empirical Bayes study and a meta-analysis agree on about 45% fewer pedestrian crashes, US only.
ranking.name: Pedestrian hybrid beacon (HAWK)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: a 4-star FHWA CMF that includes SF, contradicted by a case-crossover study against a no-facility baseline; the two use different baselines.
ranking.name: Quick-build separated bike lane (paint, flexible posts, parking protection, some concrete)

ranking.evidence_grade: low: SF's own before-and-after, confounded by the 2020 traffic drop; no published crash study of slow or neighbourhood greenway streets found.
ranking.name: Slow Streets network: a connected set of filtered or signed shared residential streets

ranking.evidence_grade: low: US manual values, mostly from rural roads
ranking.name: Stop-ahead markings and flashing beacons at stop signs

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: Danish before and after study plus TØI meta-analysis; Trafikverket warns that red-running at signals has severe consequences and SF's signalized corners already hold 66% of intersection KSI
ranking.name: Signalise a stop-controlled junction

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: TØI meta-analysis of 44 evaluations and two Danish studies, but urban effects are small and one Danish study of 149 urban conversions found injury crashes up 28%; harm to bicyclists is consistent
ranking.name: Convert a signal or stop junction to a single-lane roundabout

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate for London (several designs), but New York's first year shows no clear injury change.
ranking.name: Area cordon or congestion charge (London, Stockholm, New York, Milan Area C)

ranking.evidence_grade: low: only the hardened version shows an effect, in one NYC study; SF's painted version shows none.
ranking.name: Daylighting with a hardened corner (no parking within 20 ft, kept clear by a physical object)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: one 3-star cross-section and one 4-star state study, wide range.
ranking.name: Rectangular rapid flashing beacon (RRFB)

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: FHWA proven countermeasure with a 4-star CMF for backplates; mast-arm and Danish dark-hour results less precise
ranking.name: Retroreflective backplates, larger and extra signal heads, mast arms

ranking.evidence_grade: low: studies disagree in sign (Mishra against Avelar on all-way stops), most are on faster US roads, and the cyclist harm is large and consistent in Vancouver
ranking.name: Mini-roundabout or neighbourhood traffic circle at a stop-controlled corner

ranking.evidence_grade: moderate: two case-crossover studies agree on curb separation, but on few sites, and the Danish handbook finds urban tracks raise junction crashes unless junctions are rebuilt.
ranking.name: Curb-protected bike lane (raised or concrete-separated cycle track) on high-stress streets

ranking.evidence_grade: low: the best non-US estimate is small and not significant; LA's larger figure has no method.
ranking.name: Curb extension (bulb-out) and tighter corner radius

stacks.about: Sequential counting (TRL PPR844): within each of the 45 mode x family groups, each added fix acts only on the people left after the fixes before it, remaining = product of (1 - share x r); the package total sums over the groups. It assumes the fixes' effects are independent, the standard conservative rule. Only fixes with an annual cost and at least one computable family pair are stacked; CONFLICTS keeps one version of a fix. Shares are of 3810 people hurt and 300 KSI people a year (2017-2024 over 8). Annual cost mixes dollar years.
